name: Yellowish Orange
lede: Yellowish orange is a bright saffron yellow-orange, a descriptive name that the books use for dyes and pigments: the carrot, the crocus and a lead-chromate paint.

sections.title: A color description
sections.body: The phrase is a plain description, an orange turned toward yellow, and it appears in the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 and the Crayola lists as a near-duplicate of Signal Yellow and Bright Yellow [1]. The closest named color in our library is [[marigold]], about 4 CIEDE2000 units away [1]. The Japanese name Yamabuki-iro, for the Kerria flower, also sits at this spot [1].

sections.title: What the books call yellowish-orange
sections.body: Paterson uses the words for the carrot, noting that carrots were purple and white in Roman times and that orange became the standard around the 16th century in the Netherlands [2]. He calls saffron a yellowish-orange colorant made from the crocus [3]. The pigment books use it for chrome orange, a lead-chromate paint that the Colour Index (1971) lists as Pigment Orange 21, while the reddish one is Pigment Orange 45 [4][5]. The shade is close to [[orange]] without being it, and it is the yellow-orange end of the [[amber]] range.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This color fills at least five per cent of the canvas in 25 of 23,781 museum paintings, within six units of CIEDE2000 [6]. Most are Indian court paintings, from the Pahari and Rajput schools, such as a Krishna celebrating Holi, and 13 of the 25 date from the 1700s, about 3.6 times the archive rate [6]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings; a color match is not a pigment test [6].
